rv.q: Ms. Lavin’s performance is smaller scaled but no less affecting in its gradual revelation of the vulnerable woman beneath the polished professional.

Teacher vs. pupil. Let the conflict begin. Or in this case, the play — Donald Margulies’ "Collected Stories," in an exemplary Broadway revival which Manhattan Theatre Club opened Wednesday at its Samuel J. Friedman Theatre.

Margulies’ play certainly is schematic — the audience pretty much sees where it’s going right from the beginning — but his characterizations are so incisive and his dialogue so rich that one hardly minds.
Donald Margulies' drama delivers an engrossing, if somewhat schematic, couple of hours.
Fortunately, the stars of Lynne Meadow’s production do it for him.
But lordy, lordy, what a boring play it is.

Why, you ask, would Manhattan Theatre Club follow its premiere of Donald Margulies' Time Stands Still with a revival of Collected Stories — his crafty 1996 literary drama that's already been done twice in New York City? So we can hear Linda Lavin turn out two hours' worth of delicious bons mots like 'Life's too short for The New Yorker.
It’s skillful, diverting stuff, but essentially, light reading.
Margulies offers no reason to believe that either Ruth or Lisa has ever written a word worth publishing.
By the end of Lynne Meadow's effective production, you've gotten hooked.

cn.t: Margulies' literary drama receives a solid revival anchored by Lavin's masterful performance, though critics find the predictable mentor-protégé betrayal story more skillful craftsmanship than profound art.
